headline: Two Terminal Commands Unlock Faster Mac Keyboard Repeat Than Apple Allows
lede: macOS ships keyboard-repeat settings capped well above their hardware minimum. Two `defaults write` commands reach below the System Settings slider floor — cutting the repeat interval to 15 milliseconds and the initial-hold delay to 150 milliseconds — without installing any software.
body:
macOS's System Settings exposes keyboard repeat as a pair of sliders with a hidden floor. The *Key Repeat Rate* slider bottoms out at 30 milliseconds between characters; the *Delay Until Repeat* slider won't go below 225 milliseconds. Each integer unit in macOS's keyboard-timing system corresponds to 15 milliseconds, so `KeyRepeat -int 1` means one repeated character every 15 ms — roughly 67 keystrokes per second sustained — and `InitialKeyRepeat -int 10` sets a 150 ms hold-before-repeat delay. Apple's (AAPL) factory defaults, on Mojave and later, are a 90 ms repeat interval (value 6) and roughly 1,000 ms initial delay (value 68). The commands reduce the repeat interval to half the UI minimum and cut the initial hold time by six-sevenths.

The `defaults` command is macOS's interface to the *user defaults system*, a preferences database backed by `.plist` files in `~/Library/Preferences/`. The `-g` flag targets the *NSGlobalDomain*, a system-wide preference layer that applies to every Cocoa application that doesn't override it in its own domain. Writing `KeyRepeat` and `InitialKeyRepeat` here broadcasts the new values to Terminal, Safari, TextEdit, and most other standard apps simultaneously.

Three caveats worth knowing. The changes take effect only after a logout and re-login — the *WindowServer* reads these values at session startup, not per-app at launch. In *Electron*-based editors such as Visual Studio Code running a Vim keybinding extension, a separate flag called `ApplePressAndHoldEnabled` — introduced to surface accent-character popovers on long key presses — can disable key-repeat entirely regardless of the global `KeyRepeat` value; a separate per-app `defaults write` disabling that flag is needed alongside the global ones. Finally, games that read keyboard input through *IOKit* directly bypass NSGlobalDomain altogether, so the settings have no effect in those contexts. Users on Bluetooth keyboards may also want to soften `InitialKeyRepeat` to at least 15 (225 ms), since wireless latency can cause accidental repeats at the minimum value.

concepts.definition: macOS's built-in key-value store for application and system preferences, backed by .plist files in ~/Library/Preferences/. The `defaults` command-line tool lets you read, write, and delete these values without opening any GUI — including values the GUI doesn't expose at all.

A special preferences domain in macOS, addressable as `-g` in the `defaults` command, that stores settings shared across all Cocoa applications. Values written here act as a system-wide fallback for any app that does not define its own override in its per-app domain.

A macOS preference flag that, when true, replaces key-repeat with an accent-character popup when a key is held down — useful for entering é or ü, but it disables continuous-repeat behavior entirely. Electron-based apps like Visual Studio Code often have this set to true by default, requiring a separate per-app defaults write to restore normal key-repeat.

The macOS daemon responsible for rendering all on-screen graphics and managing input events. It reads keyboard-timing preferences at user login and applies them for the duration of the session, which is why a logout-and-login is required for `defaults write` changes to take effect.

Apple's kernel framework for device-driver communication. Games and other performance-sensitive apps often bypass NSGlobalDomain entirely by polling keyboard state directly through IOKit, reading raw hardware scan codes that are unaffected by user-defaults keyboard-repeat settings.

A framework for building cross-platform desktop applications using web technologies (HTML, CSS, JavaScript) by wrapping a Chromium browser engine. Because Electron apps don't fully follow the standard macOS Cocoa keyboard-handling pipeline, settings like ApplePressAndHoldEnabled sometimes need to be overridden on a per-app basis rather than globally.

repos.summary: A small C utility by Nikita Koekeishiya — also the author of the yabai tiling window manager and skhd hotkey daemon — that applies macOS keyboard-repeat settings at the IOKit level, instantly and without requiring a logout. It reads the same integer values as the `defaults write` commands but writes them directly to the kernel's keyboard timer. This makes it the practical solution for users who want the speed gains without rebooting.

fact_check: The commands themselves are correct, but the tweet omits a significant practical detail: the changes do not take effect until the user logs out and back in. Readers who run the commands and immediately test them will see no difference, which causes predictable confusion. The krp utility exists specifically as a workaround for this limitation, applying the change at the kernel level without requiring a session restart.
